cells.tense: Right now you're at the building of it, holding the shape and knowing that you are the one holding it.
cells.ask: Leave one thing you're carrying for someone else unfinished today, and let them pick it up.
cells.core:
You have your hands on the supports of something, and you know your own weight in keeping it steady. The care is practical and it shows — things hold up around you, and you're not guessing at what they need. At some point today, leave one thing you've been tending for someone else exactly where you stopped, unfinished, and say so out loud. What that does is let what you've built stand without you being the only reason it's standing.

You're going to feel the leaving in your chest. That's the signal the work is real, not a problem with it. If the read of you is off, the worst that happens is one person has to finish their own task — still something worth knowing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it standing. You also get to let it stand without you.
cells.verb: Tending what's been put in your hands so it can actually grow
cells.place: in the part of a life that builds the frames and patterns everything else runs on

cells.tense: You're standing a few steps into a future where you've already built all the supporting structure the present hasn't asked for yet.
cells.ask: Pick the structure you're building ahead of time and name what it's for today, before adding another piece to it.
cells.core:
You've got supports planned for things that haven't arrived, and you're keeping the whole architecture of later standing while today goes unheld. That's the strain — not the caring, which is real, but how far ahead it's aimed. When this works, you hold what's in front of you and you let the future wait its turn; the day sets the pace and you keep up with it. Today, take the structure you're most ahead of, the one you keep building in the future tense, and say out loud what it's for. Just that.

If the answer turns out to be 'nothing yet,' that's as useful as any other answer. Either way you stop building past where the load actually sits, and the present gets some of the care it's been missing.
cells.sheetLine: You've been building for a weight that hasn't arrived.
cells.verb: Tending what's been put in your hands so it can actually grow
cells.place: in the part of a life that builds the frames and patterns everything else runs on

cells.tense: You're standing at a frame you put up, and the pattern you made is still holding but you've taken your hands off it.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you hold that's gone quiet and make one small adjustment to it today, before doing anything else.
cells.core:
There's a structure you built that doesn't need your hands every minute, and somewhere along the way you stopped coming back to it. What you made still stands, which is why nobody notices, including you. At its healthiest this looks like care that doesn't clutch — you put the pattern up, you leave it to carry what it carries, and you return to it because it's yours, not because it will fall without you. Today, put your hands back on one thing you've been leaving alone and make one small adjustment. Not a rebuild — a touch.

What that changes is small, but it's yours, and small touches are how the pattern gets its keep from you again. If neither of you notices anything, at least something got handled.
cells.sheetLine: You built the pattern. Your hands have come off it.
cells.verb: Tending what's been put in your hands so it can actually grow
cells.place: in the part of a life that builds the frames and patterns everything else runs on

cells.tense: You're already the one setting the frame here, and have been for a while, without counting yourself as the one who did it.
cells.ask: Go back through one structure you live inside and point at the exact parts you built, out loud, to no one if that's what it takes.
cells.core:
The pattern you work inside has your fingerprints all over it, and you attribute it to how things ended up, to other people, to the way the job is. The building happened; the tallying didn't. When this is clean it's care that doesn't exhaust — you build the frame, you hold it while it needs holding, and you can set it down without it collapsing. Honoring what you did is just seeing it plainly, once — not forgiveness for doing it, not reward.

Today, walk through one room, project, or daily structure and name the pieces you personally put there. This is the simplest form of the thing that holds you — seeing what you've already built and letting it count. If you find less than you expected, that's a different and also useful answer.
cells.sheetLine: You built it. Time to stop saying it built itself.
cells.verb: Tending what's been put in your hands so it can actually grow
cells.place: in the part of a life that builds the frames and patterns everything else runs on
